item.title: The Sound of Silence: SAP SM49/SM69 and the OS Commands Your SIEM Never Hears
item.description:
SAP SM49/SM69 external OS command execution leaves no trace in the Security Audit Log on the most common invocation path, creating a silent blind spot most SIEM deployments never close.
- SM49/SM69 commands run via sapxpg as the sidadm OS user. The SAP Security Audit Log (SAL) records only "Transaction SM49 started" for the interactive dialog path and a generic RFC logon (AU5) for the RFC path. No event type exists in the SAL schema for the command name, binary, or runtime parameters. A SIEM ingesting only SAL sees a session open and nothing more.
- The runtime parameter string is where the real risk lives. On this SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP 7.52 system, 72 of 75 Linux-applicable shipped commands allow additional parameters at runtime. A user can point find at /tmp and pass -exec /usr/bin/id as a runtime argument. The SM69 definition never reflects this. Reviewing command definitions alone does not reveal what actually ran.
- OS auditd is the only source that captures the full argv on every path (dialog, RFC, background), because every invocation funnels through sapxpg. The verified process chain is: SAP work process → sapxpg → binary. The background job log (TBTC* tables) also records the command and parameters, but only for scheduled jobs, not interactive runs.

item.title: 2026-09-15: SmartApeSG ClickFix to unidentified RAT to MeshAgent
item.description:
SmartApeSG's ClickFix lure chains a fake browser verification page through an unidentified RAT into MeshAgent, landing a fully interactive remote access foothold on compromised Windows hosts.
Key findings:
- SmartApeSG serves a fake verification page mimicking a browser check, with embedded ClickFix instructions that trick users into manually running a malicious command (T1204.002), bypassing security prompts without any exploit required.
- The infection chain drops an unidentified RAT that establishes persistence on the host before pulling down MeshAgent, the legitimate open-source remote management tool used here as a hands-on-keyboard backdoor via a malicious Mesh C2 server.
- MeshAgent persists from AppData\Local\Temp and registers as a persistent service on the infected Windows host. That directory and run keys are your first stop. The login console screenshot confirms attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure behind it.
- All three artifact sets are available: a pcap (18.7 MB) for traffic analysis, collected malware files (34.1 MB), and a zipped IOC list, each password-protected under the site's current scheme (check the About page).
Hunt for MeshAgent binaries running from AppData\Local\Temp and unexpected outbound connections to Mesh C2 infrastructure. Parent process on the initial command execution will reflect the ClickFix run dialog. Full IOC list and pcap are in the report.

item.title: Released an open-source Windows timeline correlator (wfcr) to tackle triage fragmentation and anti-forensics
item.description:
Open-source tool WFCR correlates Windows dead-box artifacts into a single master timeline, with built-in heuristics to flag timestomping and ghost execution automatically.
Key details:
- Ingests $MFT, Shimcache (AppCompatCache), Amcache, BAM/DAM, and SRUM (SRUDB.dat) in a single offline pass, normalizing timestamps across all sources and emitting JSON Lines for Splunk, Elastic, or Sentinel, or CSV for Timeline Explorer
- Anti-forensic detection uses $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME temporal drift to catch API-level timestomping (SetFileTime), flagging manipulation that raw parsers silently miss
- Ghost execution logic cross-references Shimcache, Amcache, and BAM execution records against currently allocated MFT paths, surfacing binaries that ran and were deleted from disk, a common attacker cleanup step
- SRUM correlation dynamically resolves the SruDbIdMapTable schema at runtime rather than relying on hardcoded offsets, linking network byte transfer volumes back to specific executing binaries and user SIDs
Takeaway: if you are spending hours manually stitching CSV exports across subsystems, WFCR is worth a test run. Point it at your dead-box artifact collection and let the correlation logic surface timestamp drift and wiped payloads before you start your manual review. Validated on Python 3.10-3.12 on native Windows runners. Repo and simulated triage demo are on GitHub.

item.title: GHAPPIER - One loader, sixty-five repositories, twenty-two accounts: an unreported loader family beside DPRK's PolinRider campaign
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 loader family GHAPPIER spans 65 GitHub repos and 22 accounts, hiding inside npm supply-chain poisoning tied to the DPRK PolinRider campaign.
Key details:
- GHAPPIER operates across at least 65 public repositories, 73 infected files, and 22 GitHub accounts, giving it unusual breadth for a loader operation previously absent from public reporting.
- Initial access rides a compromised legitimate npm package whose malicious release carried valid provenance through trusted publishing infrastructure, making the payload harder to reject on reputation alone (T1195.002).
- CloudSEK links portions of this infrastructure to the PolinRider campaign, a known DPRK-attributed operation, suggesting GHAPPIER is a supporting loader layer rather than a standalone tool.
- The scale of repository and account seeding points to persistent, deliberate staging: defenders cannot treat any single repo or account as the sole exposure point.
Takeaway: audit any npm package in your environment that updated recently for signs of injected loader stages. Check GitHub dependency graphs for repos matching this seeding pattern. Full IOC list, infected file hashes, and account indicators are in the CloudSEK report; pull them before triaging affected pipelines.

item.title: Brevo Supply-Chain Attack Infected Over 100,000 Websites
item.description:
Brevo supply-chain attack weaponized a stolen Cloudflare API key to push malware through its own CDN edge to over 100,000 customer sites, with origin files untouched the entire time.
- Attackers first breached Brevo on Sept 10 via a SAML SSO vulnerability, accessing 138 accounts including Trezor's, then returned Sept 14 using a long-lived Cloudflare API key hardcoded in source code. The key carried full account permissions and let them deploy a malicious Worker, create routes, and rewrite edge responses silently, stripping CSP headers in the process. No origin file ever changed.
- The Worker modified Brevo's chat widget and tracking scripts served from cdn.brevo[.]com, injecting an additional payload loaded from sendibt1[.]com (a legitimate Brevo-owned domain, making blocklist defense counterproductive). Exposure window: 16:05 to 20:13 UTC, September 14.
- Two-stage malware payload: a ClickFix "prove you're human" overlay shown to all site visitors, and a silent WordPress plugin install triggered through active admin sessions with no password prompt. The plugin, found on VirusTotal as "Web Media Optimizer," hid from the standard plugin list, persisted via the must-use plugins folder, and beaconed a C2 server.
- Standard integrity monitoring and file hash checks would have found nothing because the attack lived entirely at the CDN layer. Hash-based controls are blind to edge-injected code.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Discovers Critical Vulnerability in libheif, the Library That Opens iPhone Photos on Your Server
item.description:
Critical CVSS 9.8 heap buffer overflow in libheif 1.18.0-1.23.2 enables arbitrary file read and RCE via a crafted HEIC upload. Actively fixed; exploitation is target-specific but demonstrably practical.
- CVE not yet public (score assigned by maintainer Dirk Farin: CVSS 9.8 Critical). Affected versions: libheif 1.18.0 through 1.23.2, but only when compiled with WITH_UNCOMPRESSED_CODEC=ON. The overflow lives in the uncompressed color-plane decoder: it reads bit-depth from the first chroma plane and uses that width to write into both planes, overflowing the second when depths differ. Attacker controls both the written bytes and overflow length through the file itself.
- The WordPress attack chain is: untrusted HEIC upload, PHP Imagick extension, ImageMagick with HEIF support, libheif. All four conditions must be true simultaneously. The official WordPress Docker image (Debian 13, libheif 1.19.8) satisfied every condition out of the box. Wordfence demonstrated protected-file disclosure and code execution on that exact deployment; a narrower copy-file test succeeded 29 of 30 attempts against a live Apache server.
- Exploitation is environment-specific but not impractical. HEIF Heist showed tailoring similar libheif bugs to a new target took roughly one to two days. Shared hosting fleets built from the same base image multiply that leverage: work done once applies to all identical deployments.

item.title: Fake LastPass Authenticator GitHub repos push new Rapuncel infostealer
item.description:
New infostealer Rapuncel pairs with a Microsoft-signed EDR killer driver to gut endpoint defenses before stealing credentials. SEO-poisoned GitHub repos impersonating LastPass and 39 other brands are the lure.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: victims land on fake GitHub repos via search, click download, get redirected to payload servers, and receive a ZIP inflated to 148MB to bypass size-based scanning. Inside, vsdbg.exe (a renamed legitimate Visual Studio debugger) sideloads vsdbg.dll, which deploys both Rapuncel and the kernel driver Alinubx.sys, disguised as an NVIDIA component nvfsflt64.sys and registering as the NvFsFilter service.
- The driver is Microsoft-signed through the Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher chain and is not currently on the vulnerable drivers blocklist. It uses ObOpenObjectByPointer with AccessMode=KernelMode to bypass PPL and terminate a hardcoded list of 145 AV and EDR processes. Defenders relying on PPL protection get no warning.
- Rapuncel harvests credentials from 25 browsers (bypassing Chrome and Edge app-bound encryption via DLL injection into the browser process), 30 crypto wallets, Discord, Steam, Telegram sessions, Windows Credential Manager, and keyword-named documents. Exfil goes to 2.26.126[.]50 over raw TCP formatted as HTTP. Persistence is a Windows service that re-kills any recovered security tools before each launch.

item.title: Attacker infrastructure, but vibe-coded: tracking the evolution of credential harvesting platforms
item.description:
AI-assisted attacker ops platforms "Loot" and "UltraVault" exposed without auth, holding 42,000+ stolen secrets including AWS keys and live AI provider credentials across 15 LLM services.
Key findings:
- UltraVault is a full post-exploitation console: one-click AWS pair correlation via /api/pairs and /api/actions/aws_pair, 14 LPE exploit recommendations per victim host, web shell re-establishment via wp_reshell and wp_rexploit, and credential minting, all accessible without authentication. Five named exploit chains are tracked internally: react2shell, wp2shell, xss2shell, joomla2shell, and deep.
- The platform's AI credential inventory spans 1,778 records across OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, and others. Only 2.7% of the 42,286 total secrets are listed as live, but the platform continuously re-probes stolen keys, including AWS Bedrock calls: GetCallerIdentity, ListFoundationModels, then InvokeModel bursts across regions in under a minute.
- Two user agents flag this activity for detection: a Boto3 client advertising kali-cloud in its platform string (os/linux.16.8+kali-cloud-amd64) and bare Python-urllib/3.13 with no SDK. Temporary STS credentials with ASIA-prefixed access key IDs were also actively validated by the same host.

item.title: Nozomi identifies 12 vulnerabilities in Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403, enabling root access and OT network attacks
item.description:
12 vulnerabilities in Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 enable chained root access, telemetry manipulation, and lateral movement across OT networks. Patch to firmware V4.0 HF0 or above immediately.
- CVE-2025-40572, CVE-2025-40573, and CVE-2025-40574 chain to escalate a read-only local account to root on the LPE9403 (CVSS up to 8.5). From there, an attacker controls telemetry before it reaches SCADA, falsifying sensor values and suppressing alarms while the physical process runs in an unsafe state.
- If SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client V2.1 or below is installed, CVE-2025-40582 (command injection) lets a compromised SINEMA server push root commands to every connected LPE device. One rogue server becomes multi-site OT compromise. CVE-2025-40581 adds authentication bypass; CVE-2025-40583 exposes credentials in cleartext.
- The second attack path requires only SSH access plus the SINEMA auth bypass to redirect the client to an attacker-controlled server, triggering the command injection and achieving root without touching the SINEMA infrastructure at all.
- Impact at root: credential and config exfiltration, network mapping of OT assets, service disruption, and persistent footholds that bridge separate OT segments for lateral movement.
Update SCALANCE LPE9403 firmware to V4.0 HF0, segment the device from untrusted networks, and audit SINEMA Remote Connect server trust relationships.

item.title: Sysmon Modular, a new toolkit for building and tuning your configuration
item.description:
Sysmon Modular gets a Go-native toolkit for building, validating, and diff-ing configurations, plus new modules covering AI agents, credential artifacts, and browser extensions.
Key details:
- The core utility is now a single Go binary with no third-party dependencies, shipping prebuilt for Windows, Linux, and macOS on x64 and ARM64. It replaces the older PowerShell and Python scripts as the supported path. Commands cover merge, validate, diff, analyze, and coverage, with ATT&CK Navigator layer output defaulting to ATT&CK 18.
- The diff command compares parsed rule expressions and their Boolean grouping rather than raw XML text, so an AND-to-OR change stays visible while a formatting change does not. The analyze command flags hazardous exclusions such as a well-known binary excluded by filename alone rather than full path, which can suppress a different binary using that name from an unexpected directory.
- New modules cover security-control changes, credential artifacts, browser and editor extensions, and AI agent execution, including Claude, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, and others launched as node.exe. Four FileCreate (Event 11) modules track agent configuration and hook files, mapped to T1546, consistent with MITRE now explicitly listing AI coding-agent hook persistence.
- Pre-built consolidated configs move to GitHub Releases, built by CI/CD for Sysmon 15.21, 14.16, 13.34, and 12.03. Update any automation pulling raw-repository URLs.

item.title: Beware the SparroWock: The backdoor that bites, the commands that catch
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT FamousSparrow deploys new SparroWocky backdoor against Latin American governments, replacing SparrowDoor as its primary implant since August 2025.
- FamousSparrow pivoted geographically hard: 90% of targets from mid-2025 into 2026 are Latin American government entities across Argentina 🇦🇷, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras 🇭🇳, Panama, Peru 🇵🇪, Puerto Rico, and Venezuela. ESET ties this to China 🇨🇳's reaction to US 🇺🇸 pressure in the region, including Panama's legal challenge to a Chinese-operated port concession. Initial access via exploiting public-facing Exchange servers (T1190).
- SparroWocky is a distinct C++ backdoor, not a SparrowDoor variant. Deployed via DLL side-loading trident loader (T1574.001): legitimate EXE, patched malicious DLL (seen as winfsp-x64.dll, DukeQt.dll), and RC4-encrypted .dat payload file. Magic bytes MZ/PE are stripped from the in-memory payload to evade scanners. SHA-1 of primary sample: 44F0A22B143B79FA760BF31E14C8FFF714C8A2A1.
- Evasion stack is deep: SilentMoonwalk call stack spoofing, MinHook hooking CreateThread to display AnimateWindow as thread start address, custom API hashing (T1027.007), and forged PEB_LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY structures to hide reflectively loaded PEs. BOF execution (command 0x14) via embedded COFF Loader lets operators run Cobalt Strike-compatible modules in-process.

item.title: From Registry-Stored PowerShell to In-Memory Cryptocurrency Mining: A Multi-Stage Infection Chain
item.description:
XMRig cryptominer delivered through a five-stage chain using Registry-stored PowerShell, DNS TXT C2, and .NET assemblies hidden inside PNG and WAV files, all executing fully in memory.
- Registry key HKLM:\Software\uf42a9660377\vstdfehzr holds a binary-encoded PowerShell payload executed via vstdfehze.ps1 with -executionPolicy Bypass. DNS TXT queries to sslvalidcert[.]com, later txtcdn[.]net and httptls[.]org via DNS-over-HTTPS, resolve C2 addresses and steer payload delivery, using an X-HWID header to track infected hosts.
- PNG steganography: frames-1zm.pages[.]dev/frames.png carries a hidden script in the red pixel channel. WAV files (Atsg.wav, Tmav.wav, Realtek HD Audio.wav from publicwavlib.pages[.]dev) embed .NET assemblies in the lower nibbles of audio bytes past the 44-byte header, all loaded via [Reflection.Assembly]::Load() with nothing written to disk.
- Persistence is layered: hidden Scheduled Tasks run the encrypted payload at logon and on interval; a WMI permanent event subscription fires on a Registry condition change. Defender exclusions are added broadly, PowerShell history is wiped, and telemetry is weakened via a .NET DLL loaded in-memory.
- Final payload is XMRig (RandomX rx/0), configured remotely via config-rg7.pages[.]dev/config.txt. WinRing0.sys is dropped for MSR access. C2 at 104.21.2[.]193:8443 persists independently of mining, meaning the host stays controllable even after the miner is found.

item.title: MikroTrick: Inside the RouterOS Takeover Chain
item.description:
MikroTik routers were being exploited before patches went public. Bishop Fox reproduced the full unauthenticated takeover chain and found persistence artifacts on real compromised devices that survive a patch.
Key findings:
- The attack chain is unauthenticated, meaning no credentials are needed to gain control of the router. Exploitation happened before fixes were publicly available, placing every exposed MikroTik device in the window of risk regardless of patch timing.
- Bishop Fox recovered persistence artifacts on real-world compromised devices, confirming attackers were not just popping shells and leaving. Responders cannot treat a patched router as a clean router without investigating what was left behind.
- The reproduction of the full takeover chain gives defenders a concrete attack path to model detections against. The methodology matters here: the chain exists, it works, and it was used in the wild before defenders had a patch to apply.
- RouterOS forensics are non-standard. Evidence lives in the router's file system, scheduler jobs, user accounts, scripts, and firewall rules. These artifacts do not surface in traditional endpoint telemetry and require direct device inspection.
If you manage MikroTik devices, patching is not enough. Pull the user list, scheduler entries, scripts, and firewall rules from every device and compare against a known-good baseline.

item.title: 100,000 WordPress Sites Exposed to Remote Code Execution via PHP Object Injection Vulnerability Found by Wordfence Argus in Tutor LMS
item.description:
CVE-2026-78175 (CVSS 8.8): PHP Object Injection in Tutor LMS lets any subscriber-level user achieve full RCE on 100,000+ WordPress sites via a serialization length-desync and GuzzleHttp POP chain.
- CVE-2026-78175, CVSS 8.8 (High). Affects Tutor LMS versions 4.0.7 and below. The entry point is the tutor_save_withdraw_account AJAX handler in classes/Withdraw.php, which lacks a capability check and relies solely on a nonce that any logged-in user can obtain from the homepage. Since most Tutor LMS installs enable open student registration, an anonymous visitor can self-register and immediately exploit the flaw.
- The root cause is esc_sql() misapplied to values destined for update_user_meta(). WordPress internally expands each % character to a 66-byte HMAC token, serializes the inflated string, then collapses the token back on DB write, leaving serialized length declarations 65 bytes larger than actual content. A second request triggers unserialize() on the corrupted blob, over-reading into attacker-controlled POST keys and materializing injected objects.
- The POP chain works by injecting a reference to ecommerce\PaymentGateways\Paypal\vendor\autoload, which the plugin's spl_autoload_register loader in classes/RestAPI.php resolves and includes, bootstrapping the bundled Guzzle autoloader.

item.title: EtherHiding Exposed: Inside a Blockchain-powered Malware Campaign Hiding in Plain Sight
item.description:
A BEC investigation uncovered a blockchain-powered C2 campaign active since November 2025, using Polygon smart contracts to store live C2 addresses across 31 compromised websites, with a backdoor now delivering a real-time banking trojan targeting 479 financial domains.
- EtherHiding on Polygon: the C2 agent holds nine hardcoded Polygon RPC endpoints and sends a read-only eth_call to a smart contract to retrieve an encrypted C2 domain, decrypted with a repeating-key XOR (key: $%)W$fgl34). item.title: Unpacking a laZzzy Donut
item.description:
Six-stage loader chain pairs Python obfuscation with Donut shellcode and laZzzy PE encryption, fully unpacked via static analysis without executing the payload.
- The chain opens with a heavily obfuscated Python script that decodes through multiple layers before dropping an encrypted blob. Each stage exists to burn analyst time and evade automated sandboxes that give up before the final payload surfaces.
- Donut is the shellcode generation framework at the heart of this chain. It converts PE files into position-independent shellcode for in-memory execution, leaving no dropped binary on disk (T1620). That makes filesystem-based detection and most sandbox verdicts blind to the final payload.
- laZzzy handles the PE encryption wrapping the inner payload. It uses XOR and AES to protect the payload until runtime, so static AV signatures on the final executable are useless until each layer is manually peeled back.
- The full six-stage sequence was reconstructed without execution, using static Python deobfuscation and manual shellcode parsing. This matters for DFIR: sandbox-evading loaders can still be fully analyzed if you work the layers offline rather than waiting for runtime behavior.
Prioritize memory forensics on suspected hosts: Donut payloads land in injected or hollowed processes and never touch disk. Dump process memory and scan for Donut shellcode headers.

item.title: The skb that wasn't freed - the Fragnesia primitive via Open vSwitch
item.description:
New LPE bug family: Open vSwitch strips SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG from a live forwarded skb, reopening the Fragnesia page-cache write primitive. Deterministic root on default Arch, Fedora, Debian, Amazon Linux, and RHEL with no race condition required.
Tracked as CVE-2026-90049, CVE-2026-89487, and CVE-2026-80977. Public since 2026-08-13, fixed in mainline and stable on 2026-09-04. Actively exploitable on unpatched kernels today.
- Root cause is in queue_userspace_packet() inside net/openvswitch/datapath.c. When an OVS upcall fails, skb_tx_error() calls skb_zcopy_clear(), which clears the entire SKBFL_ALL_ZEROCOPY group including SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG. Because do_execute_actions() ignores the upcall return value, the same skb, now missing its ownership marker but still carrying foreign page-cache frags, continues down the action pipeline to OUTPUT. If that output reaches esp_input(), the gate at skb_has_shared_frag() passes and the in-place AES-GCM decrypt writes attacker-controlled plaintext directly into the page-cache folio.
- Exploitation requires three things an unprivileged user can satisfy: CAP_NET_ADMIN inside a user namespace (GENL_UNS_ADMIN_PERM on all OVS genl ops, so unshare -Urn is enough), openvswitch.ko autoloading on first genl family resolution (no CAP_SYS_MODULE needed), and an MSG_ZEROCOPY send over a PROT_READ MAP_SHARED mapping of a root-owned file so SKBFL_DONT_ORPHAN keeps the page-cache frag from being copied during the upcall.

item.title: How I Tricked OpenClaw Into Attacking Its Own Network: A NAT64 SSRF Bypass
item.description:
A parser-differential bug in OpenClaw's SSRF guard let a crafted NAT64 IPv6 literal route to 169.254.169.254 while showing the guard a harmless 8.8.8.8. Fixed in v2026.8.1.
- OpenClaw (formerly Clawdbot/Moltbot) is an always-on AI gateway running inside user trust boundaries with a web_fetch tool, image-URL ingestion, and inbound media resolution. Every one of those is an SSRF primitive if the address guard can be fooled.
- The guard correctly decoded IPv4-mapped, 6to4, Teredo, and the well-known 64:ff9b::/96 NAT64 prefix. The flaw: ipaddr.js v2.4.0 folds the RFC 8215 64:ff9b:1::/48 prefix under the same "rfc6052" label. The guard read parts[6]/parts[7] (the trailing 32 bits) for both, but in the /48 layout the real embedded IPv4 lives in hextets 3-5. The trailing bits are RFC 6052-mandated ignored suffix, meaning attacker-controlled scratch space.
- The crafted address 64:ff9b:1:a9fe:a9:fe00:808:808 embeds 169.254.169.254 in the correct /48 slots and places 8.8.8.8 in the ignored suffix. Guard sees 8.8.8.8 and passes. A real NAT64 router decodes 169.254.169.254 and forwards there. Precondition: host must have an actual 64:ff9b:1::/48 NAT64 gateway present.
- Patch is in v2026.8.1 and all later releases. Affected builds confirmed: beta range 2026.7.2-beta.1 through 2026.8.1-beta.2, with possible earlier stable versions still under review.
Hunt tip: if you build SSRF guards, audit any case where a library classification label implies a memory layout.

item.title: TrustSink: How a Rogue External MFA Provider Steals Passwords

Because prl_disp_service launches tar as root, the attacker's compress-program script runs as uid 0. No VM needs to be running.

item.title: Detections Digest #20260914
item.description:
Weekly detection engineering digest covers 38 rule changes across 7 repos, with standout additions for ClickFix, RMMmax, email evasion, and LLM prompt injection.
- Splunk added a ClickFix rule correlating RunMRU registry writes (Sysmon Event ID 13) with browser clipboard events (Sysmon Event ID 24) by matching SHA256 hashes of copied payloads, a clean two-event join that confirms a user ran exactly what the browser put on their clipboard. The PowerShell 4104 hunting rule was also updated to fix wildcard syntax for credential dumping keywords and base64 indicators, including patterns tied to CVE-2025-59287.
- LOLRMM added four Sigma rules for RMMmax covering process execution of RMMmaxAgentSetup.exe and RMMmaxAgentService.exe, Run key and service registry persistence, file drop artifacts, and C2 network traffic to RMMmax infrastructure. Sublime also dropped the screenconnect.com domain restriction so ScreenConnect guest-access parameter detection now catches self-hosted deployments serving .msi and .exe files.
- Sublime added 11 email rules targeting PDF passcode lures, dub.sh links in attachments, BEC Excel files with legal disclaimers, fake Cloudflare verification pages loading client.js or the CF beacon, and ICS calendar invites faking file-share notifications.

item.title: Threat Hunting with JA4/JA4S (+ Practical KQL Queries)
item.description:
JA4/JA4S TLS fingerprinting brings a more durable hunting signal to Microsoft Defender and Entra ID logs, surfacing unusual clients and servers that IP and domain IOCs miss entirely.
- JA4 is human-readable, not just a hash. The first segment of a fingerprint like t12d180700_4b22cbed5bed_2dae41c691ec decodes directly: TCP, TLS 1.2, SNI present, 18 cipher suites, 7 extensions, no ALPN. This lets hunters query individual fields rather than exact hashes, making baselining and anomaly detection far more flexible than JA3 ever allowed.
- In EntraIdSignInEvents, the GatewayJA4 field exposes the client fingerprint for every sign-in. Parsing it with KQL to extract TLSVersion, CipherCount, ALPN, and the cipher/extension hashes lets you cluster sign-ins by client behavior. SNI absent ("i") or ALPN of "00" in a sea of h2 sign-ins is the kind of outlier worth pulling for review.
- DeviceNetworkEvents carries both JA4 and JA4S inside AdditionalFields for TLS-inspected connections. JA4 tells you about the client; JA4S tells you about the server that answered. Pairing them lets you profile both sides of a session and spot mismatches, unusual server responses, or automated tooling.
- The FoxIO JA4+ mapping CSV can be pulled via externaldata() and joined to enrich fingerprints with known application, library, and OS context. Match rates are low in practice, but a hit on a known C2 framework or unusual library is valuable pivot.

item.title: Google Doc Sidebar Sends Mac and Windows Users Down Different Paths to Malware
item.description:
A crypto-themed X lure used a live Google Doc with a bound Apps Script to fingerprint, triage, and route victims to OS-specific malware, including a rogue CA that survives process kill and partial cleanup.
Key details:
- The Google Doc sidebar was a Google Apps Script running client-side in the browser. Opening the doc while signed in, clicking nothing, triggered a VIEW beacon over Telegram that reported the victim's IP, geolocation, browser, and installed crypto wallet extensions (MetaMask, Phantom, Tron, Solana). Passive document viewing is passive recon delivery.
- Windows victims faced a three-stage PowerShell loader chain pulling encrypted payloads, ClickOnce abuse to install a fake "Google API Connector" signed with a stolen Norwegian 🇳🇴 company cert, and a distraction fake progress bar. Three code-signing certs were abused total, including one stolen from Discord Inc.
- The most dangerous final-stage payload hollowed MsBuild.exe and installed a self-signed CA presenting as Google Trust Services (CN=WR3), a fabricated www.virustotal[.]com leaf cert, a hosts-file entry, and a LocalProxy firewall rule. The CA is regenerated per host, so thumbprint blocklists are useless. The CA, hosts entry, and firewall rule all survive reboot even after the process dies.
- macOS victims received an AMOS infostealer variant via piped zsh or a DMG from GitHub, targeting keychain, browser data, cookies, Telegram, Apple Notes, and crypto wallets.

item.title: Attackers Actively Exploiting Critical Vulnerability in WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-27540 (CVSS 9.8): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture lets attackers drop PHP webshells and achieve full RCE. Actively exploited, 100k+ blocked attempts since February.
- CVE-2026-27540 affects the wwlc_file_upload_handler AJAX endpoint, reachable with zero authentication. The flaw: allowed file types are read from the attacker-controlled file_settings POST parameter, not server-side config. An attacker simply includes "php" in that forged JSON list, bypasses extension checks, and uploads a .php webshell directly into the WordPress uploads directory. test_type is explicitly set to false in the upload call, killing WordPress's own MIME check too.
- Real attack traffic shows POST requests to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with action=wwlc_file_upload_handler carrying shell.php, a webshell that fingerprints the host and provides a browser upload form for staging further payloads. Top offending IPs: 92.241.13[.]213, 31.59.129[.]150, 2a0f:85c1:840:5389[.]1, 92.241.13[.]140, 23.137.105[.]214.
- Exploitation peaks hit June 4-17, July 1, and August 30, 2026. Roughly 6,000 installations are exposed. Patch version 2.0.3.2 exists; anything at or below 2.0.3.1 is vulnerable.
Grep web server access logs for POST /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php containing wwlc_file_upload_handler, then audit wp-content/uploads for unexpected .php files and review wp_users for unknown administrator accounts added post-compromise.

item.title: Gamers Get Played: Fake GTA6 Leaks Deliver a Grab Bag of Malware
item.description:
Fake GTA6 ISOs weaponized with four malware families hit Eastern Europe-adjacent gamers, combining RATs, a credential grabber, and a destructive Chaos ransomware wiper in a single installer.
- Infection starts when a victim mounts the ISO and runs gta6installer.exe, which displays a Russian-language "unlicensed copy" warning and pre-conditions the victim to expect a "License not found" failure. That failure is then deliberately triggered by find.vbs via WScript.exe, masking successful malware execution behind an anticipated error. Files drop to %TEMP% under names mimicking GTA, Rockstar, Steam, and Windows components.
- Four payloads deploy in parallel: NJRAT (multiple instances including license.exe, rockstargamescrashfixer.exe, rockstarservices.exe) adds firewall rules and beacons to AWS IPs and the ngrok tunnel 7.tcp.eu.ngrok[.]io:12684. DCRAT drops as UserOOBEBroker.exe under C:\Users\Default\Local Settings\ and phones home to a0700877.xsph[.]ru. Mercurial Grabber (adminapp.exe) exfiltrates Discord tokens, Chrome creds, Minecraft and Roblox session data via a Discord webhook.
- Chaos ransomware (gta6.exe) acts as a wiper: it requires admin rights, deletes shadow copies, disables recovery, encrypts files under 200 MB with AES using a random 20-char key, and overwrites larger files with random data. No payment mechanism exists. The read_it.txt ransom note is cosmetic cover for pure destruction.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Identifies Two Critical Unauthenticated Vulnerability Chains Leading to Remote Code Execution in The Events Calendar Plugin
item.description:
Two unauthenticated RCE chains (CVSS 9.8) in The Events Calendar WordPress plugin threaten 600,000+ sites. Both fire through pending-comment preview with zero login required, patched in version 6.17.4.1.
- CVE-2026-78006 (CVSS 9.8): PHP Object Injection via is_safe_widget_instance() in Service_Provider.php. The guard calls unserialize() with allowed_classes => false, but PHP fires __unserialize() and __wakeup() magic methods during pre-parse before the return value is checked. A malformed tail token causes the guard to see false, declare the payload safe, and forge a valid wp_hash(). Core's real unserialize() then constructs Lazy_Post_Collection, whose custom_unserialize() passes attacker-controlled 'callback' and 'ids' directly to array_map(), enabling OS command execution as the web server user.
- CVE-2026-78159 (CVSS 9.8): Arbitrary-callable RCE via Element_Classes::parse_array() in common/src/Tribe/Template.php. A plain array bypasses the object guard entirely. Attacker-controlled 'classes' keys reach parse_array(), which calls is_callable() without restricting to closures. Supplying wp_update_user with ID and user_pass entries resets the admin password to a known value; attacker logs in and uploads a malicious plugin.
- Shared entry point: get_v1_single_event_html() buffers the full page including comments and passes it through do_blocks(). WordPress's KSES sanitizer preserves HTML comment delimiters, so Gutenberg block markup survives.

item.title: HBO Max ads on a compromised Reddit account exposed a massive PasteSwitch ClickFix operation
item.description:
A hijacked, verified Reddit account for HBO Max ran 108 ClickFix malvertising ads in 48 hours, exposing PasteSwitch: a cross-platform delivery operation serving macOS stealers, Windows loaders, and blockchain-controlled crypto clippers.
- The u/hbomax account was compromised and used to buy legitimate Reddit ads pointing to hbomaxx[.]us and four other lure domains. Victims who clicked were shown a ClickFix overlay instructing them to paste a terminal or Run dialog command, bypassing browser download protections entirely. On macOS, curl|zsh chains dropped MacSync (exfiltrating browser creds, Telegram data, Apple Notes, and passwords via /tmp/osalogging.zip) or an AMOS helper persisting as .com.apple.accountsd, polling /api/join/ and /api/tasks/<bot-id>.
- On Windows, mshta fetched an MP3/HTA polyglot (hash: 5e8ad983129f6771d186f60379dca30d208374cac45bac75d5459aaf0fabc8ad), created a scheduled task, launched 32-bit PowerShell, disabled AMSI, and injected Amatera Stealer (d4eb6e4cec1e69f3bc94bbe2d743e982863fc8549e49f832846c218e1aba3fcb) directly into memory. Amatera connected to 77.91.65[.]13:443 while presenting facebook.com as the TLS SNI, causing network logs to record a Facebook connection instead of the real C2.
- AnimateClipper and ZigClipper used Binance Smart Chain contracts (AnimateClipper: 0x6936edc505501EBB2F202C985a021a06f1c10C9E) to store the live C2 domain, calling getData() on-chain.

item.title: ATT&CK grew a 15th tactic: A practical DFIR field guide to the Stealth / Defense Impairment split
item.description:
ATT&CK's Defense Evasion tactic is now two: Stealth (TA0005) and Defense Impairment (TA0112). The split forces distinct evidence collection strategies and changes how you report detection coverage across 15 Enterprise tactics.
Key details:
- Stealth (TA0005) covers blending in: timestomping with $SI vs FN mismatches in the MFT, alternate data streams, masquerading, packing. Artifacts live on disk and in the file system. Hunt with MFTECmd, USN parser, and YARA. USN journal gaps are a strong signal.
- Defense Impairment (TA0112) covers actively breaking telemetry: event log clears (Event ID 1102), Defender registry tampering, firewall modifications, stopped security services. Evidence is louder but attackers will try to destroy it. EvtxECmd and RECmd are your primary tools.
- In cloud and identity environments the footprint shifts entirely. Stealth looks like a valid session token with broad access. Defense Impairment looks like disabled conditional access or muted alerting policies. Artifacts move to sign-in logs and unified audit trails, no timestomping or log clearing to hunt.
- The full 15-tactic field guide maps forensic artifacts and tooling per phase, built from Sophos IR engagements. Cross-cutting: KAPE and Velociraptor for triage, Plaso for supertimelines, Sigma and ATT&CK Navigator for coverage mapping.
Re-tag anything mapped to old Defense Evasion into TA0005 or TA0112 now. Your coverage reporting is wrong until you do.

item.title: When the web shell isn’t on disk: the F5 BIG-IP rootkit that lives in memory
item.description:
An F5 BIG-IP APM rootkit (named PoisonedRefresh by ESET) hooks Apache and PHP at runtime to serve a web shell that never touches disk, exploiting CVE-2025-53521, an unauthenticated RCE now in CISA KEV.
- CVE-2025-53521 is the door. An unauthenticated RCE in BIG-IP APM, added to CISA KEV in March 2026 after active exploitation was confirmed. F5 initially misclassified the severity, correcting it only after weaponization was observed. The implant arrives as a second-stage payload post-exploitation, meaning initial access is already behind you by the time the rootkit appears.
- The implant is a stripped, statically linked ELF that hijacks __libc_start_main to hook apr_dso_load, then waits for libphp to load. It intercepts Apache's file reads for apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, and webtop_popup_css.php3, substituting a malicious in-memory version. The on-disk file, its hash, and FIM alerts all stay clean. T1505.003 assumed the shell was findable on disk. This breaks that model.
- A second access path creates a Unix domain socket at /run/bigtlog.pipe. After a token check, connections are redirected to /bin/bash. No TCP listener, no reverse shell to an external IP. Network monitoring sees nothing unusual.
- The related installer can infect the Apache binary and persist through BIG-IP upgrade images. Rebooting or upgrading does not guarantee remediation, and it destroys the volatile evidence that explains what happened.

item.title: LNK Metadata
item.description:
LNK metadata goes far deeper than the embedded command line. The RustGate v2 delivery file exposes machine ID, MAC address, SID, volume serial, and shell item timestamps that fingerprint the attacker's build environment.
- The LNK for RustGate v2 shows working dir C:\Windows\Temp, basepath rundll32.exe, and a command line pulling hxxp://5.252.177[.]210:8090/test.bat via curl before executing it minimized. Icon spoofed as msedge.exe to deceive the victim.
- Shell item timestamps inside the LNK recorded rundll32.exe with a creation time of 2025-12-02, while Windows and System32 show 2024-04-01 creation, giving a bracketed window for when the LNK was staged on the threat actor's machine.
- The TrackerDataBlock names the build host "server" and records MAC address 00:50:56:c0:00:08 (a VMware NIC prefix), placing LNK creation inside a VM. The PropertyStoreDataBlock adds a user SID (S-1-5-21-2202213833-2675363039-2741304641-1002) and a parsing path under C:\Users\Public\Pictures, narrowing the actor's environment further.
- All metadata fields are fully populated, meaning the actor used no sanitization tool. Comparing these values across multiple LNK files from the same campaign allows clustering, as JPCERT/CC and APT29 researchers demonstrated: identical machine IDs, MACs, or volume serials link files even when hashes differ.
Parse every LNK with LECmd or a purpose-built tool and record all data blocks, not just the command line.

item.title: Smish. Click. Drained: Inside the Smishing Triad’s Phishing Cockpit
item.description:
The Smishing Triad's JWR phishing kit gives operators a live cockpit to steer victims through credential and card theft in real time, a technical leap beyond static phishing pages.
Key details:
- JWR kit communicates between operator and victim via encrypted WebSockets, letting the Outsider operator cluster intercept OTPs, replay credentials, and redirect victims mid-session without reloading the page. This is active adversary-in-the-middle, not passive harvest.
- AES-256-CTR encrypts the kit's communications, making network-layer inspection of the session content significantly harder. Defenders relying solely on payload inspection will miss the exfiltration channel.
- The kit is multi-stage: smishing lure leads to a branded phishing page, victim input is relayed live to the operator cockpit, and the operator drives the next prompt (card details, OTP, address) based on what the victim submits. Each stage is a separate artifact opportunity.
- Infrastructure artifacts matter here. WebSocket upgrade requests, short-lived domains mimicking postal and banking brands, and the operator panel's login page are the fingerprints to hunt.
Hunt your proxy and DNS logs for WebSocket upgrade requests (HTTP 101) to recently registered domains impersonating delivery or financial brands. TLS certificate transparency logs are a useful pivot. Full IOC list and operator infrastructure indicators are in the Group-IB report.

item.title: SETTRA RANSOMWARE
item.description:
Settra, a ransomware group active since June 2026, has claimed 64 victims across the US 🇺🇸, Germany 🇩🇪, UK 🇬🇧, and Canada 🇨🇦, exfiltrating up to 3.2TB per target while deliberately avoiding healthcare.
- Settra operates its own DLS at settra5ldqwgtw5q7z5awbsvlksakyfojuc5slgrz5lvapune4fantqd[.]onion and a negotiation panel at settra5ceeidlmbt2d7zupsb3r7djl2azjj4mho5kznmdap6vnoxoxqd[.]onion, both running nginx and protected by Anubis proof-of-work (EdDSA/Ed25519 JWT). File servers are separate non-vanity onion nodes, three active now after migrating from four deprecated nodes in late August 2026.
- The ransom note drops as RESTORE_FILES.txt and instructs victims to log into the negotiation portal using a "LOGIN ID." A secondary "Return Key" is generated on first login to gate session continuity, meaning researchers replaying the Login ID get a fresh key and lose access to prior chat history. TOX handle D288571294F08ADDFE46DF631194745143BE8B40F9F846379040DC40EB39BC2E8CE056B66927 is the out-of-band contact.
- Victim profiling on the DLS is AI-assisted, surfacing financial balance sheets, bank names, insurance payouts, and employee termination letters. Infostealer credentials are assessed as a likely initial access vector for roughly 50% of victims, consistent with the breadth of targets across sectors and geographies.
- Ten victims including zayo[.]com (460GB) and medevolve[.]com (820GB) have been de-listed, suggesting ransom payment or a pressure tactic.
